A churn model predicts who is likely to leave under the observed policy; a retention system needs to know whose outcome an intervention can change. Estimate treatment effects from randomized offers/contact experiments where possible, including a no-treatment control. High-risk users may be impossible to retain, while low-risk users may stay without a discount.

Choose actions by expected incremental retained value minus offer/contact cost, subject to eligibility, capacity, and fairness constraints. Treatment definitions and outcome windows must be stable. Uplift estimation requires overlap and valid causal assumptions; it is not automatically superior when treatment data are sparse, biased, or the intervention is ineffective.

Use separate data for policy learning and evaluation, and evaluate incremental profit/retention through experiments or justified off-policy methods. Monitor harms such as teaching users to threaten churn for discounts. A conservative fallback can use broad eligibility rules until treatment evidence accumulates. Report uncertainty and subgroup effects rather than presenting every individual uplift score as a known causal fact.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For action a, compare expected incremental retained value $v(x)\tau_a(x)-cost_a(x)$ with the no-action baseline. Uplift estimates are conditional averages, not observable individual counterfactual truths. Validate the chosen policy on independent randomized data where possible, including uncertainty, offer capacity, and adverse behavioral effects of repeated incentives.
